findings.title: Unauthenticated raw error exposure with inconsistent handling (id=27 errorHandlingChallenge)
findings.analysis: Unauthenticated GET requests hit two distinct raw error paths that return non-graceful, inconsistent server errors instead of sanitized user-facing messages. GET /rest/user/security-question (no email param) returns 500/2946 B with a raw Sequelize WHERE error ('WHERE parameter "email" has invalid "undefined" value') plus a full stack; GET /redirect (with continue param) returns 500/2531 B with a raw TypeError. Both triggers reproduce byte-stably across fresh requests on this boot (GET /rest/user/security-question sha256 0b84d83c08cc28421da7b67c32d997676e490f8bd4016854f849200c2e11a90b x3; GET /redirect sha256 020023ff4f9ae2b934531ecd4f7f04d012a055a23b67e99de52dbc3f7ec4ec48 x3). The raw errors expose internal SQL syntax/line-level detail. Inconsistency is proven on the same application: graceful 'Unexpected path' wrappers and 401 denials appear on other routes, so the raw-500 responses are not uniform error handling but a specific failure mode. Target: http://lab-mutator:3000.
findings.false_positive_check: Benign control check: the same GET on /rest/user/security-question with a valid email returns 200 with structured question JSON (not an error), proving the 500 is triggered by the missing parameter rather than generic broken routing. The /redirect TypeError is distinct from the graceful 'Unexpected path' 500 wrappers seen on other unimplemented routes. Both 500 bodies are raw server exceptions, not sanitized responses. SHA256 byte-stability across 3 fresh requests rules out one-off noise.

findings.title: Unauthenticated exposure of Prometheus telemetry with LLM usage gauges (id=97 exposedMetricsChallenge)
findings.analysis: GET /metrics returns 200 text/plain (~26134 B) unauthenticated, serving Prometheus-format application telemetry including http_requests_count (2XX/3XX/5XX), process_*, nodejs_version_info, juiceshop_version_info, and juiceshop_llm_* token gauges (input/output tokens, tool calls) plus juiceshop_challenges_solved counters. All four gauge families verified present in the response body. No secret/token/key lines present in the raw body (secrets scan clean). Unauthenticated observability leakage can aid attacker reconnaissance (version fingerprinting, request-rate baselining, AI-feature discovery). Target: http://lab-mutator:3000.
findings.false_positive_check: No authentication header required; the endpoint is deliberately public (a baseline Juice Shop feature), but the exposure includes LLM usage counters and challenge-solved counters that go beyond generic uptime telemetry — the leaked counters are the distinct, security-relevant element and are reproducible fresh on the target.

findings.title: Unauthenticated exposure of full nested user objects in a public collection (excessive data exposure)
findings.analysis: GET /rest/memories returns 200/6183 B unauthenticated with 10 records, each carrying a full nested `User` object (field: User) containing email, a 40-hex password hash, role, a 40-hex deluxeToken, totpSecret, lastLoginIp, plus other PII (username, profileImage, createdAt). The shape persisted across repeated fresh requests (verified req1 and req2). Because the collection is unauthenticated, any visitor receives complete user objects — exposing password hashes and token material that is typically only available after authentication. Note: on this boot the User object is nested under the `User` key (prior boots flattened the fields); the exposure class is unchanged.
findings.false_positive_check: A bogus Bearer token returns the identical 200/6183 B response, proving the exposure does not depend on authorization at all. The nested structure is the application's own serialization of related records, not a crafted injection. Fresh requests preserve the sensitive fields, so this is not transient leakage.

findings.title: Unauthenticated write-open / read-gated authorization gap on /api/SecurityAnswers/ (UserId=null)
findings.analysis: GET /api/SecurityAnswers/ returns 401 'UnauthorizedError: No Authorization header was found', but an unauthenticated POST to the same route with a minimal body (questionId + answer) returns 201 'success' with a server-assigned id (id 24 on first probe, id 25 on repeat — id increments across requests) while UserId is null and SecurityQuestionId/answer fields are null. Parallel read-gated write-open on the same route demonstrates a client-side authorization bypass: write state is accepted and persisted without ownership binding (UserId:null) or question linkage. Target: http://lab-mutator:3000.
findings.false_positive_check: Benign control: a properly authorized write (with a valid Authorization header) would bind UserId; here the same request without any auth header succeeds with unbound (null) ownership. The read side remains gated (401), so the gap is specifically write-open/read-gated rather than full enumeration. Repeat POSTs produce fresh server ids, proving acceptance-and-persistence rather than a transient acceptance of junk.

findings.title: Account-existence disclosure and question-text enumeration via unauthenticated security-question endpoint
findings.analysis: GET /rest/user/security-question?email= returns a deterministic body shape that discriminates account existence: an existing configured account (bjoern@owasp.org, emma@juice-sh.op) returns 200 with {question:{id, question, createdAt, updatedAt}} (e.g., id=7 'Name of your favorite pet?', id=10 'Company you first work for as an adult?'), while an unknown email returns 200/2 B {}. A non-configured but syntactically valid email still yields the empty-object shape, so the differential is between known configured accounts and everything else — usable for account enumeration and as a foothold for further targeted attacks (e.g., the exposed question text supports security-question answering/credential-reuse attacks). Target: http://lab-mutator:3000.
findings.false_positive_check: The two body shapes (question JSON vs {}) are deterministic and structurally distinct, not timing- or size-based side channels. Repeated fresh requests reproduce both shapes; the non-existent address always returns the exact 2-byte `{}`. The endpoints neighbors (authentication-details 401, other /rest/user/* 500) are gated, proving the differential is specific to this route and not generic leakage.

findings.title: CAPTCHA answer revealed in cleartext on the public CAPTCHA endpoint (id=7 captchaBypassChallenge partial)
findings.analysis: GET /rest/captcha returns 200/47 B with {captchaId, captcha: <arithmetic expression>, answer: <cleartext computed answer>} — the server's own computed answer is exposed in the response body (e.g., captcha '5-1*8', answer '-3'; verified: 5-1*8 = -3). captchaId increments on each request (6 -> 7 across probes), proving server state and non-static content. The cleartext answer nullifies the CAPTCHA's purpose (proving human interaction) for any requestor of the endpoint.
findings.false_positive_check: Arithmetic verification independently computes the claimed answer (5-1*8 = -3 matches the server's 'answer' field), so this is a genuine answer leak, not random noise. The full bypass path (posting the answer to submit feedback) is broken in this mutation variant (all POSTs to /api/Feedbacks/ return 500 raw captchaId error), so the claim is limited to the answer-leak vector, which is itself a security-relevant control bypass.
